sources.title: NPR Topics: Home Page Top Stories

articles.author: Diane Webber
articles.description: Sen. Chris Murphy is expected to fully recover from his stroke. The acronym BE FAST can help you remember the symptoms of stroke and what to do when it happens: Call 911 quickly.
articles.title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember

articles.author: Barbara Sprunt
articles.description: Rep. Haley Stevens was scheduled to attend a unity event today with Abdul El-Sayed, who beat her in the Democratic primary. Instead, she endorsed his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
articles.title: Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate in Michigan Senate race, spurning Abdul El-Sayed

articles.author: Eric McDaniel
articles.description: Murphy's office says he was taken to the hospital this weekend after experiencing numbness in his arm. His chief of staff said he is responding well to treatment and expected to make a full recovery.
articles.title: Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy is hospitalized with a stroke

articles.author: Domenico Montanaro
articles.description: Polls show Democrats with an advantage in the midterm election but there are potential limitations and results may take a while to roll in.
articles.title: How to think about the midterms — and the political moment the country is in

articles.author: Hansi Lo Wang
articles.description: A federal judge has dismissed a highly unusual lawsuit by the Trump administration that tried to block the certification of results from Alaska's U.S. Senate race if the Republican incumbent lost.
articles.title: Judge tosses Trump's attempt to block Alaska Senate results if GOP incumbent loses

articles.author: Ron Elving
articles.description: At least some portion of the nation is likely to have its political confidence — and perhaps even its sense of security — tested in the days and weeks ahead. That test could also continue for some time to come.
articles.title: The midterms will test the nation's political direction and confidence

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the men's race of the New York City Marathon in his debut in the event while Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won the women's race on Sunday for the second time.
articles.title: New York City Marathon: Sweden's Almgren and Kenya's Chepkirui win as 60,000 take part

articles.author: Julie Appleby
articles.description: The ACA health insurance marketplaces — find yours at HealthCare.gov — open Nov. 1 for 2027 coverage. Getting an early start may be especially important this year.
articles.title: It's ACA open enrollment time. Here are the changes for health insurance shoppers

articles.author: Elena Moore
articles.description: On the eve of what may prove to be a tough election for the GOP, young conservatives vying to be part of the first class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress want a role shaping the party's next chapter.
articles.title: How Gen Z Republicans running for Congress are thinking about the future of the party

articles.author: Maham Javaid
articles.description: As polls close on election night, here's a look at what to expect each hour and which midterm races are key to deciding control of Congress.
articles.title: Here's how to watch election night as the polls close, hour-by-hour

articles.author: Rachel Hall
articles.description:
Exclusive: Professional bodies call for regulation to boost confidence and protect public from abuse in ‘landmark’ report
Ministers should introduce statutory regulation for counsellors and psychotherapists to protect the public from abuse, according to a report that has been hailed as a “watershed moment” for the profession.
Unlike most other healthcare roles, including doctors, midwives and osteopaths, “psychotherapist” and “counsellor” are not protected titles nor statutorily regulated professions in the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Counsellors and psychotherapists call for UK statutory regulation in ‘watershed moment’

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Judicial commission finds against Vicky Prapas over a series of comments, including one made when school children were present

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A magistrate who told a court user “I want to slap you around a bit, too” has come under fire for her offensive and inappropriate language.
The remark was one of several made by Victorian magistrate Vicky Prapas that the state’s judicial watchdog has found to be inappropriate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I want to slap you around a bit, too’: Victorian magistrate reprimanded over language in court

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
‘I’m just happy to catch fish,’ Matthew Maurice says after landing 80cm barramundi as part of Northern Territory competition

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Darwin man is $1m richer after angling an 80cm, red-tagged barramundi during a night-time fishing trip with his brother.
Matthew Maurice, a 26-year-old from the Northern Territory, had finished football training and decided to take a boat out on Thursday evening with his sibling, who was visiting from overseas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Million-dollar fish caught by Darwin man ‘just fishing and talking’ at night with brother

articles.author: Ima Caldwell and Penry Buckley
articles.description:
Deployments of surveillance vans over five months result in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

More than a million people have had their faces scanned in a trial of real-time facial recognition technology in Western Australia, resulting in 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts.
WA police said under the five-month trial, which concluded on Saturday, the technology scanned 1,380,882 faces after 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests

articles.author: Roque Planas
articles.description:
President again took aim at progressive Senate candidate and lauded Haley Stevens for endorsing Mike Rogers
Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”.
Trump’s comments aimed to influence a neck-and-neck race that will play an outsized role in determining which party controls the senate after Tuesday’s midterm elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say

articles.author: Chris Hippensteel and Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Endorsement was met with backlash from the party, condemning Stevens for her ‘betrayal’
Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.
Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’s endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers

articles.author: Tess Ikonomou
articles.description:
‘My political career may die,’ senator says after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, will run for a lower house Queensland seat at the next federal election but will avoid having to face off against a key One Nation figure.
Canavan confirmed his bid following the announcement that Capricornia MP Michelle Landry will retire, leading to speculation it could be a tight race with Pauline Hanson’s national director.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pauline Hanson and James Ashby rule out running against Nationals leader Matt Canavan in Capricornia

articles.author: Eric Berger
articles.description:
Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage
A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents to sue OpenAI earlier this week.
The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately led to their death.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parents of woman who died of seizure after ChatGPT misguidance sue OpenAI

articles.author: Natricia Duncan in St John's, Antigua
articles.description:
British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda 
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom international airport and was headed to the Bahamas when it crashed 
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway, killing everyone onboard.
Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach county roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: All nine people aboard business jet that crashed in Florida have died

articles.author: Imogen Tilden
articles.description:
Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.
The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final

articles.author: Chris Hippensteel
articles.description:
Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses

articles.author: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Move to scrap legal requirement to set aside water for environment is ‘extreme even for the NT CLP government’, green group says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Northern Territory government has been accused of making a “blatant and shameless” attack on nature by planning to delete a legal requirement that water must be allocated to the environment.
In what has been described as the latest in a series of attacks on the environment by the NT’s Country Liberal party, the Finocchiaro government plans to change water rules that govern how much ground and surface water industry can take.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Northern Territory water plan condemned as ‘blatant and shameless’ attack on nature

articles.author: Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh
articles.description:
MPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandal
Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.
Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK

articles.author: Haroon Siddique
articles.description:
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.
Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.
Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz

articles.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
articles.description:
Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.
Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries

articles.author: Kiran Stacey, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme

articles.author: Jon Henley in Paris
articles.description:
Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania 
French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.
Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi

articles.author: Eduardo Porter
articles.description:
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Cryptocurrency exchange says 90% of losses covered as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor

The cryptocurrency exchange Binance has started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack.
The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Binance resumes customer withdrawals after record $6.3bn hack

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’
Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.
Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
articles.description:
Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income
North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme

articles.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.
Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report

articles.author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
articles.description:
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts
Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities

articles.author: Ollie Lewis for MetDesk
articles.description:
Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected
Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan
The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.
Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says

articles.author: Libby Brooks
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment
Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.
UK politics | John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
Patrick Stewart | The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, died at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said.
Environment | One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.
Europe | Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.
US news | The Trump administration has opened a criminal investigation in California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Durban Deep
articles.description:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi
articles.description:
Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job

articles.author: Amy Hawkins in Beijing
articles.description:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials

articles.author: Julian Borger in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority

Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
Musician wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US president
Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.
The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.
But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
You can push us to the brink
But where the open road divides
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song

articles.author: Peter Beaumont
articles.description:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothing
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India

articles.author: Mark Townsend
articles.description:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’

articles.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
articles.description:
Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders
Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says

articles.author: Amrit Dhillon in Delhi
articles.description:
Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’

articles.author: Agence France-Presse in Yangon
articles.description:
Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years

articles.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Michael Lewis; produced by Saskia Collette and Ross Burns; executive producer Homa Khaleeli and Sami Kent
articles.description:
What happens when Elon Musk and a bunch of tech bros try to rip up the US government?
Journalist Michael Lewis – the author of Moneyball and of The Big Short – talks to Nosheen Iqbal about his new book Blockers, which tracks the story of the civil servants who stood up to Elon Musk’s ‘department of government efficiency’ as it tried to dismantle the US government. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The ‘blockers’ who stood up to Elon Musk’s Doge – podcast

articles.author: Roque Planas
articles.description:
President again took aim at progressive Senate candidate and lauded Haley Stevens for endorsing Mike Rogers
Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”.
Trump’s comments aimed to influence a neck-and-neck race that will play an outsized role in determining which party controls the senate after Tuesday’s midterm elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
On stage in Iowa, Trump praised congresswoman Haley Stevens’ defection from the Democrats to support Mike Rogers' Senate campaign – going so far as to welcome her to join the Republican party. He then called Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim, a 'jihadist,' continuing a line of a Islamophobic attacks against the progressive Democratic Senate nominee.

Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally


Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump praises Haley Stevens' defection while lobbing Islamophobic insults at El-Sayed – video

articles.author: Chris Hippensteel and Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Endorsement was met with backlash from the party, condemning Stevens for her ‘betrayal’
Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.
Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’s endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers

articles.author: Chris Hippensteel
articles.description:
Incumbent Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results after ‘unprecedented intervention’ by Trump’s DoJ
A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses

articles.author: Roque Planas
articles.description:
Democratic senator was at his son’s hockey game when he felt a numbness in his arm and was in Johns Hopkins 
Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke.
Murphy, 53, started feeling numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday, according to the Connecticut senator’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. A hospital visit confirmed that Murphy had experienced a stroke.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Connecticut senator Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke

articles.author: Ella Baron
articles.description: Continue reading...
articles.title: Ella Baron on Donald Trump and the US midterms – cartoon

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
Voters are turning against the Republicans. But the clearest possible message is needed to safeguard democracy
The psychologist Jennifer Freyd identified a pattern often used by perpetrators: deny, accuse, and reverse victim and offender. More than one observer has noted that Donald Trump employs that pattern politically. With polls suggesting Republicans are likely to lose the House and perhaps the Senate too in the midterms, the man who refused to accept Americans’ democratic verdict in 2020 is hawking a narrative of cheating Democrats who will steal seats via illegitimate votes.
The January 6 insurrection showed how acute the peril to American democracy had become. It is more so now. This time, Republican efforts to undermine the results began well in advance. In 2020, Mr Trump’s vice-president, Mike Pence, the attorney general, William Barr, and others refused his most outrageous demands; now the justice department is supine. And the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, which safeguarded against the worst kinds of racial discrimination, means that states no longer require pre-approval for decisions that could well tilt a race. Districts have already been redrawn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms and election interference: Trump’s attempted heist is already under way | Editorial

articles.author: Prachi Gupta
articles.description:
In state that has become ‘ground zero’ for discrimination against south Asians, experts say they are seeing voters motivated to fight back
Last winter, while Pooja Sethi was canvassing to become the Democratic candidate for the Texas house of representatives, she received a text from a staff member alerting her to a post on X. The Turning Point USA influencer Savanah Hernandez – a Trump supporter known for creating videos that target immigrants – had posted a photo of Sethi’s campaign banner with the caption: “Welcome to politics in Texas.”
The post went viral.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘There’s a lot of hate’: rightwing racism stirs south Asian mobilization in Texas

articles.author: James Rosen
articles.description:
Trump’s utter abuse of the power proves it. As the midterms approach, voters have not forgotten January 6
From betraying Ukraine and dispatching masked agents who killed Americans to deporting US citizens and pulling out of accords controlling climate change and Iranian nuclear weapons, the list of Donald Trump’s abuses is long and growing still longer, seemingly by the day.
Looking back decades from now, historians will see that at the top of this shameful list is Trump’s utter abuse of his pardon power. It started on the first day of his second term, when he pardoned more than 1,500 insurrectionists who, on 6 January 2021, had stormed the US Capitol.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon power | James Rosen

articles.author: Stephen Starr in Springfield, Ohio
articles.description:
Haitian community in Springfield demands dignity and better rights for immigrants as ICE crackdown ramps up
Michaelle Louis’s feet and legs are aching. She can barely walk.
Surrounded by corn fields and the distant hum of a busy highway, the native of Haiti and dozens of other activists are 23 miles into a 45-mile march from Springfield to Ohio’s statehouse in Columbus to demand better rights for Haitian immigrants.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We spend our days in silence’: fear and repression in Ohio as ICE terrorizes Haitian immigrants

articles.author: Jason Wilson
articles.description:
One man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political funding system
In the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to a Super Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.
The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwing Utah senator Mike Lee.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns

articles.author: Michael Sainato
articles.description:
Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising prices
For millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.
In Lorain county, Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and on pace to break the US record for longest public sector strike.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Affordability top of mind for voters in final sprint to midterms: ‘I have to pick between medicine or groceries’

articles.author: Dave Schilling
articles.description:
From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous
Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.
After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.
Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling

articles.description:
Donald Trump attacked the appearance of a Reuters reporter and called him 'disgusting' after the reporter asked a question about the president's cancellation of two upcoming campaign events. A day later, Trump rescheduled the canceled rallies in Kansas and Iowa.

Trump lashes out at Reuters reporter who asked why he canceled rally in Kansas

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'You look like hell': Trump blows up at reporter when asked about canceled events – video

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland , with Carrie Dann, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
There are 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 in the Senate and 39 governorships up for grabs in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Jonathan Freedland is joined by Carrie Dann, of the Cook Political Report, to run through some of the races to watch before the final weekend of campaigning
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Final countdown to the make-or-break midterms – podcast

articles.author: Oliver Laughland, Tom Silverstone, Jem Talbot, Katie Lamborn
articles.description:
Democrats have failed to win statewide office in Texas for 30 years. Before the midterms, Oliver Laughland and Tom Silverstone travel to San Antonio to follow James Talarico and Ken Paxton on the campaign trail - to find out whether the state's Senate race is really up for grabs, how Elon Musk's millions are affecting the race and whether voters have changed their minds on Trump

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Democrats win against Elon Musk's millions in Texas? – video

articles.author: Rachel Hall
articles.description:
Exclusive: Professional bodies call for regulation to boost confidence and protect public from abuse in ‘landmark’ report
Ministers should introduce statutory regulation for counsellors and psychotherapists to protect the public from abuse, according to a report that has been hailed as a “watershed moment” for the profession.
Unlike most other healthcare roles, including doctors, midwives and osteopaths, “psychotherapist” and “counsellor” are not protected titles nor statutorily regulated professions in the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Counsellors and psychotherapists call for UK statutory regulation in ‘watershed moment’

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn

articles.author: Natricia Duncan in St John's, Antigua
articles.description:
British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda 
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda

articles.author: Imogen Tilden
articles.description:
Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity
A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.
The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final

articles.author: Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh
articles.description:
MPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandal
Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.
Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK

articles.author: Haroon Siddique
articles.description:
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.
Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure
National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.
Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her

Reeves says UK’s future is in the EU

Which senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”
It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, in a lecture six months ago.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government

articles.author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Arrests come ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on the direct action group
Police have said they arrested 325 people on Saturday at a demonstration outside the US embassy in London against the proscription of Palestine Action.
In updated arrest figures released on Sunday, the Metropolitan police said 320 people were detained outside the building in Battersea, south London, for allegedly expressing support for an organisation banned under the Terrorism Act.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police detain 325 people at pro-Palestine Action protest at US embassy in London

articles.author: Kiran Stacey, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme

articles.author: Charlie Moloney
articles.description:
Police searching for ‘unknown group’ that gained entry to property in Chandler’s Ford on Saturday night 
Five teenage boys were stabbed at a Halloween party, after an “unknown group” gained entry to the event on a residential road, police have been told.
The boys, all aged 16 and 17, were found injured after police were called to a report five teenagers had been stabbed at a property in Chandler’s Ford near Eastleigh, Hampshire, just after 10.30pm on Saturday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Five teenagers hurt in stabbing at Halloween party in Hampshire

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
Adrian Ramsay says some new members would be ‘more at home’ in Your Party or Socialist Workers party
Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader of the Green party of England and Wales, has said the party must fix its internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying that some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.
Ramsay, who has been critical of the handling of the row over a “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green party conference, said there were a “small number” of individuals who used “divisive” tactics to influence the party’s agenda.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Green party must avoid being taken over by hard left, says former leader

articles.author: Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent
articles.description:
Holyhead, Tremadog and Bangor UPCCs may shut as Betsi Cadwaladr University health board struggles with funding
A struggling Welsh health board could close urgent primary care centres at three hospitals, citing funding and recruitment issues, prompting widespread criticism.
Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, which serves about a quarter of Wales’s population, said it was consulting on ending urgent primary care centres (UPCCs) at Ysbyty Penrhos Stanley in Holyhead, Ysbyty Alltwen in Tremadog and Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor by April 2027.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Welsh health board considers closing urgent primary care centres at three hospitals

articles.author: Rob Davies
articles.description:
Hundreds of adult gaming centres in England have bingo licences that still qualify them for discounted business rates
Hundreds of high street “slot farms” could continue claiming a discount on their business rates, unless the government closes a loophole that allows them to pose as bingo halls.
John Healey singled out adult gaming centres (AGCs) in his first budget this week, in which he increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25%, claiming he was “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: High street ‘slot farms’ could avoid budget tax rise through bingo hall loophole

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
In the final article in a series on high-end British manufacturing we look at a clothing brand that dates to the 18th century but is increasingly on-trend

Making jeans again: the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan

Rolls-Royce rides high on craze for customisation

Luxury leather: from wallets to cigar cases

Tina is wielding a large pair of scissors with authority, slicing with immense skill and precision.
With 38 years of experience, she is an important member of the 230-strong manufacturing team producing fine knitwear for the John Smedley brand. Using a chalk, a semi-circular guide and a sharp pair of scissors, she cuts necklines in the knitted garments ready for the final trim to be attached.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
Chancellor John Healey fails to guarantee equalisation with adult wage will happen in timeframe set out in manifesto
Labour looks less likely to meet its manifesto pledge to equalise the minimum wage for younger workers before the next election, after the chancellor failed to guarantee the rise would happen within that timeframe.
John Healey said on Sunday his party was “prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government”, including possible spending cuts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour’s pledge to level-up minimum wage for under-20s before next election in doubt

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
Tory leader says apology would be ‘navel-gazing distraction’ and would be used as lever for financial compensation
Kemi Badenoch has said an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.
Speaking to broadcasters on Sunday, Badenoch also questioned whether it was worth future leaders attending the Commonwealth summit, given that it was now dominated by calls for reparations.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Britain should not issue apology over slave trade, says Kemi Badenoch

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

articles.author: Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent
articles.description:
Natural Resources Wales says short-necked oil beetle has been found in country for first time in nearly 60 years
A rare beetle has been rediscovered in Wales after nearly 60 years, conservationists have said.
The short-necked oil beetle, driven to the brink of extinction in Britain due to habitat loss over the course of the 20th century, has been found at the Castlemartin range in Pembrokeshire, according to Natural Resources Wales (NRW).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rare beetle that oozes substance from its knees when attacked rediscovered in Wales

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
Former chancellor says leaving European Union has made Britain ‘poorer, weaker and less secure’
The former chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued Britain’s future should be back in the European Union, saying Brexit has made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Andy Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith, executive producers Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale.
articles.description:
What if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, Brexit, levelling up – and still failed to increase growth per person in the UK. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode of Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty, rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
You can watch previous episodes of Radical Thinking here
  

  
Aditya’s suggested reading list for this episode:
 

 

 As we say in the podcast, I’ve championed the work of Karel and Sukhdev and their colleagues for many years in the Guardian, and some of my columns are a good introduction to their approach.
In our conversation we look at what life after growth looks like for towns and suburbs, and what it should look like. This report from south Wales in 2016 examines the present-day reality.
For a broader analysis of how the UK has become highly unequal and increasingly stagnant, try this.
As part of the Foundational Economy Collective, Williams and Johal put a lot of their analysis into freely available working papers. That circumvents the leisureliness and expense of academic publishing and gets their arguments in front of a wider public. A good example is this one on the cost of living crisis.
More recently, they’ve focused on the broken water system of England and Wales in a book called Murky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.
The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights

articles.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
articles.description:
London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open
Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works.
Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption

articles.description:
What if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, UK governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, leaving the EU, levelling up, and they have still failed to increase growth per person. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode, the rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain to Aditya Chakrabortty why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life

Aditya’s suggested reading list for Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal:

As we say in the podcast, I’ve championed the work of Karel and Sukhdev and their colleagues in the Guardian for many years, and some of my columns are a good introduction to their approach.

• In our conversation we look at what life after growth looks like for towns and suburbs, and what it should look like. This report from South Wales in 2016 examines the present-day reality.

• For a broader analysis of how the UK has become highly unequal and increasingly stagnant, try this.

• As part of the Foundational Economy collective, Karel and Sukhdev put a lot of their analysis into freely available working papers. That circumvents the leisureliness and expense of academic publishing and gets their arguments in front of a wider public. A good example is this one on the cost of living crisis.

• More recently, they’ve focused on the broken water system of England and Wales in a book called Murky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System.

Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round!”
It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer, as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”.
 

 

 In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing.
But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit, meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.
Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. articles.description:
AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games. Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from.
Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video, which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more.

Happy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, and shiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got to powerwash her house?

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.
That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

articles.description:
Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.
Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.
